rewrites.summary:
No division-specific transgender evidence appears in the surviving sources; a visitor here stands under the national framework as it operates countrywide.

As those sources establish: same-sex activity is not criminalised, but the 2023 laws ban same-sex marriage and legal gender recognition; the 'extremism' designation has produced 101 convictions since early 2024, with 'propaganda' penalties surging to 257 in 2023-24; official asylum guidance singles out trans people, open activists and one conflict-affected region cluster for heightened risk.

As the sources establish: a foreign government's travel advisory warns that 'propaganda'-law convictions can bring arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation for foreigners, and that displaying rainbow symbols is itself criminal; the 2023 laws ban legal gender recognition; the extremism designation has produced 101 convictions since early 2024.
rewrites.blindSummary: No division-specific evidence; national framework applies: the 2023 marriage and gender-recognition bans, extremism-designation prosecutions (101 convictions since 2024), and foreign-advisory warnings of arrest, short detention and deportation under the propaganda law for symbol display or 'promotion'.
blindSourceSummaries: Foreign government travel advisory for this country (retrieved via audit): propaganda-law convictions of foreigners can bring arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation; symbol display including the rainbow flag is treated as criminal.
Human-rights organisation report (June 2025): 101 extremism convictions since the 2024-effective movement designation; propaganda penalties 257 in 2023-24 versus 22 in 2021-22.
Official asylum guidance (June 2025): 2023 laws ban same-sex marriage and gender transition; trans people and open activists face heightened risk notwithstanding generally unstated state risk.

rewrites.summary:
No division-specific transgender findings appear in the surviving sources; the national mechanisms they document apply here unchanged.

In short: prison placement follows the legal sex on identity documents (Criminal Procedure Code art. D248), so trans women are typically housed in men's facilities; the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté reports persistent serious violations of trans detainees' rights across inspected prisons and names them the group that suffers most in custody.
rewrites.blindSummary: No division-specific findings in the surviving sources; national mechanisms apply unchanged: document-sex-based prison placement (criminal-procedure code provision), and the national detention inspectorate's finding of persistent serious violations against trans detainees across inspected facilities.
blindSourceSummaries: Investigative prison feature (Jan 2018): placement follows the sex on identity documents, so most trans women are held in men's facilities; first-person accounts of hostility in custody; the national detention inspectorate calls trans detainees the group that suffers the most in prison.

National detention inspectorate opinion (May 2021): on some forty referrals since 2010 and on-site inspections, serious violations of trans detainees' fundamental rights persist across places of deprivation of liberty; recommendations extend to intersex and non-binary people.
